questions.stem: A 38 year old woman has had 1 week of tiredness, and today her gums started bleeding and she has bruises on her arms and legs. Her temperature is 37.1°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 116/72 mmHg. Her blood film shows numerous abnormal promyelocytes with Auer rods and some fragmented red cells. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her bleeding?
questions.e: Acute promyelocytic leukaemia is a classic trigger of DIC, giving low platelets and fibrinogen, raised D-dimer and prolonged PT and APTT. ITP causes isolated thrombocytopenia.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of her bleeding? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Haematological malignancy** (promyelocytic leukaemia) with low platelets, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer and prolonged clotting times.

elim: An inherited isolated factor VIII deficiency with a prolonged APTT only, presenting in childhood.
Causes low platelets with normal PT, APTT and fibrinogen.
Prolongs PT but does not cause low platelets, low fibrinogen or fragmented cells.
An inherited mucosal bleeding disorder with normal platelets and fibrinogen.

steps.x: **A. Disseminated intravascular coagulation.** Malignancy, especially haematological, is a classic DIC trigger alongside sepsis, trauma and obstetric causes.

questions.stem: A 27 year old man is in intensive care after a motorcycle collision with pelvic and femoral fractures and a crush injury to his leg. He has received 2 units of red cells. On day 1 he starts to ooze from his wounds, cannula sites and urinary catheter. His pulse rate is 118 bpm and BP 98/60 mmHg. He takes no medicines. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Major trauma triggers DIC: microthrombi consume clotting factors and platelets, causing bleeding from multiple sites. Two units of red cells are not enough to cause dilutional coagulopathy.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: pelvic and femoral fractures and a crush injury
ooze from his wounds, cannula sites and urinary catheter
steps.x: Major **trauma**, bleeding from **multiple sites** and consumption of platelets and clotting factors.

elim: He has had only 2 units, which is not enough to dilute clotting factors and would not raise D-dimer this much.
Would cause an isolated prolonged APTT with normal platelets and fibrinogen.
Occurs 5 to 10 days after heparin, causes thrombosis rather than oozing, and clotting times are normal.
Causes isolated thrombocytopenia with normal clotting.

steps.x: **B. Disseminated intravascular coagulation.** Trauma releases tissue factor and triggers DIC; consumption of factors causes bleeding.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman suddenly becomes breathless and hypotensive during labour, shortly after her membranes rupture. She is resuscitated and delivers by emergency caesarean section. An hour later she is bleeding from the wound, her cannula sites and her gums, and the uterus is well contracted. Her pulse rate is 130 bpm and BP 82/48 mmHg. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her bleeding?
questions.e: An obstetric catastrophe such as amniotic fluid embolism triggers DIC, causing bleeding from multiple sites with low fibrinogen and platelets and high D-dimer. A contracted uterus excludes atony.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of her bleeding? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: bleeding from the wound, her cannula sites and her gums
steps.x: Sudden collapse in labour (likely **amniotic fluid embolism**), then bleeding from **multiple sites**.

elim: Causes isolated thrombocytopenia; her clotting times and fibrinogen are abnormal too.
Causes uterine bleeding, not oozing from the wound, cannula sites and gums.
The uterus is well contracted, and atony does not cause bleeding from cannula sites.
An inherited cause of mucosal bleeding; it does not suddenly cause low fibrinogen and high D-dimer.

steps.x: **A. Disseminated intravascular coagulation.** Obstetric catastrophes (abruption, amniotic fluid embolism) are classic DIC triggers.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man is in hospital with sepsis from a urinary source. On day 2 his platelets have fallen to 31 ×10⁹/L, his PT and APTT are prolonged, his fibrinogen is low and his D-dimer is markedly raised. He reports bleeding gums. His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 112 bpm and BP 96/58 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of his skin?
questions.e: DIC consumes platelets and clotting factors, giving a petechial rash, purpura and easy bruising. Erythema nodosum and target lesions belong to other conditions.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on examination of his skin? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Sepsis-triggered **DIC** with low platelets and consumed clotting factors.

elim: Tender red nodules on the shins, linked to sarcoidosis and inflammatory bowel disease.
A lace-like rash seen in antiphospholipid syndrome and vasculitis; not the typical DIC skin finding.
A sign of chronic liver disease.
Seen in erythema multiforme.

steps.x: **D. Petechiae and purpura.** DIC skin: petechial rash, purpura and easy bruising.

questions.stem: A 59 year old woman has septic shock from pneumonia. Her haemoglobin has fallen and her blood film shows schistocytes. Her temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 120 bpm and BP 88/54 mmHg. She is not confused and has no history of diarrhoea. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her blood film appearance?
questions.e: Schistocytes with prolonged PT and APTT, low fibrinogen and raised D-dimer in sepsis indicate DIC. TTP and HUS also cause schistocytes, but clotting is normal.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of her blood film appearance? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Schistocytes **plus** prolonged PT and APTT, low fibrinogen and high D-dimer, in **sepsis**.

elim: Gives spherocytes and a positive direct antiglobulin test, not schistocytes.
Follows bloody diarrhoea, usually with renal failure and normal clotting.
Causes low platelets without red cell fragmentation or clotting abnormalities.
Causes schistocytes and low platelets, but PT, APTT and fibrinogen are normal.

steps.x: **B. Disseminated intravascular coagulation.** Schistocytes with deranged clotting = DIC; schistocytes with normal clotting = TTP or HUS.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man with metastatic pancreatic cancer has a swollen left calf, confirmed as a deep vein thrombosis. A week later he develops bruising, nosebleeds and oozing from venepuncture sites. He has no fever and is not on anticoagulants. His pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 128/78 mmHg. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Metastatic cancer triggers widespread activation of coagulation, forming thrombus and then consuming platelets and clotting factors so the patient bleeds. ITP does not cause thrombosis or deranged clotting.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Malignancy** causing both **thrombosis and bleeding** with consumed platelets and fibrinogen.

elim: He is not on heparin.
Causes isolated low platelets with normal clotting and D-dimer.
Would prolong PT, but not cause this degree of D-dimer rise and thrombocytopenia with thrombosis.
Prolongs PT but leaves platelets and fibrinogen normal and does not cause thrombosis.

steps.x: **A. Disseminated intravascular coagulation.** DIC = widespread activation of coagulation: thrombus formation with consumption of platelets and factors.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man has septic shock from a perforated diverticulum and has DIC with platelets 28 ×10⁹/L, prolonged PT and APTT and low fibrinogen. Despite antibiotics and fluids, his urine output falls to 10 mL/hour, his creatinine rises from 90 to 260 µmol/L and he becomes confused. His BP is now 104/62 mmHg on noradrenaline.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his worsening organ function?
questions.e: In DIC, microthrombi form throughout the microcirculation and reduce organ perfusion, causing organ dysfunction and multi-organ failure. A single local cause would not explain both kidney and brain.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of his worsening organ function? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
DIC with **organ dysfunction** in more than one organ.

elim: No contrast is mentioned, and this would not explain his confusion.
Would not explain the kidney injury.
Possible for the kidney, but would not explain the multi-organ picture.
A catheterised septic patient with falling output across organs; nothing suggests obstruction.

steps.x: **C. Microthrombi in the microcirculation.** DIC can progress to multi-organ failure as microthrombi block small vessels.

questions.stem: A 78 year old woman with E. coli sepsis from cholangitis develops visible haematuria on day 2. She also has bleeding gums and a petechial rash. She was catheterised without difficulty on admission and has no history of urinary symptoms. Her temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 116 bpm and BP 94/56 mmHg. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her haematuria?
questions.e: Sepsis is the most important trigger of DIC, which causes bleeding from multiple sites including haematuria, gum bleeding and petechiae. Local urological causes would not explain bleeding elsewhere.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of her haematuria? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: bleeding gums and a petechial rash
steps.x: **Sepsis** with bleeding from **multiple sites** (urine, gums, skin) and deranged clotting.

elim: She has no urinary symptoms and this would not cause bleeding gums or abnormal clotting.
Would not explain the bleeding gums, petechiae and deranged clotting.
The catheter went in easily, and it would not cause gum bleeding.
Causes pain and haematuria, not bleeding from multiple sites.

steps.x: **D. Disseminated intravascular coagulation.** Sepsis is the most important trigger of DIC; bleeding is from multiple sites.

questions.stem: A 21 year old woman has meningococcal septicaemia. She is in intensive care on noradrenaline. Her fingertips and toes have become cold, dusky and mottled while her radial and pedal pulses remain palpable. She also has purpura on her legs. Her platelets are 22 ×10⁹/L, fibrinogen is 0.5 g/L and D-dimer is markedly raised.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of the changes in her fingers and toes?
o: Acute embolism to both arms and legs
Microvascular thrombosis from disseminated intravascular coagulation
questions.e: DIC forms microthrombi throughout the microcirculation, which can cause digital ischaemia while large vessel pulses remain present. Emboli to large vessels would cause absent pulses.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of the changes in her fingers and toes? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Sepsis, **consumed** platelets and fibrinogen, and **small vessel ischaemia** with preserved pulses.

elim: Large vessel emboli would cause absent pulses; hers are palpable.
No cold exposure is described.
Episodic colour change on cold or stress, not persistent ischaemia with purpura and deranged clotting.
Seen in young male smokers and develops over months.

steps.x: **C. Microvascular thrombosis from disseminated intravascular coagulation.** DIC is clotting AND bleeding: microthrombi block small vessels while consumption causes bleeding.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man is on day 3 of treatment for pneumonia with sepsis. He is on prophylactic enoxaparin, started on admission. He now has bleeding from his cannula sites and a petechial rash. His temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 114 bpm and BP 92/56 mmHg. He has no new swelling of his limbs. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Sepsis is the most important trigger of DIC, which causes consumption of platelets and clotting factors with bleeding. HIT occurs later, causes thrombosis and does not prolong clotting times.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: day 3 of treatment for pneumonia with sepsis
steps.x: **Sepsis**, bleeding, and the full consumption pattern on the coagulation screen.

elim: Usually 5 to 10 days after starting heparin, causes thrombosis rather than bleeding, with normal clotting and fibrinogen.
Causes isolated thrombocytopenia with normal PT, APTT and fibrinogen.
Prophylactic doses do not cause low platelets, low fibrinogen and high D-dimer.
Leaves platelets and fibrinogen normal.

steps.x: **A. Disseminated intravascular coagulation.** Sepsis is the most important trigger of DIC.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman has a placental abruption at 34 weeks. After delivery she oozes from her cannula sites and has a petechial rash. Her pulse rate is 122 bpm and BP 90/54 mmHg. Her full blood count shows platelets of 44 ×10⁹/L. The obstetric registrar suspects disseminated intravascular coagulation.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
o: Coagulation screen with fibrinogen and D-dimer
questions.e: The coagulation screen is the gold standard for DIC, showing low fibrinogen, prolonged PT and APTT and raised D-dimer. A platelet function assay does not assess factor consumption.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Suspected **DIC** after an obstetric catastrophe; confirm consumption of clotting factors.

elim: Used to investigate marrow failure or malignancy, not to confirm DIC.
Tests for immune haemolysis.
Used for haemophilia A.
Tests platelet function, not consumption of clotting factors.

steps.x: **B. Coagulation screen with fibrinogen and D-dimer.** Gold standard: coagulation screen (low fibrinogen, low platelets, high D-dimer, prolonged PT and APTT).

questions.stem: A 49 year old man is in intensive care with septic shock from a perforated bowel. He is oozing from his line sites and his platelets are 34 ×10⁹/L. His PT and APTT are prolonged. A coagulation screen is sent, including a D-dimer.
questions.q: Which is the most likely D-dimer result?
o: Raised only if a deep vein thrombosis is present
questions.e: In DIC, fibrin clots form throughout the microcirculation and are broken down by fibrinolysis, so D-dimer is markedly raised. A normal D-dimer would argue against DIC.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely D-dimer result? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Widespread clot formation means widespread **fibrinolysis**.

elim: D-dimer is high from fibrinolysis regardless of anticoagulation.
Ongoing clot formation and breakdown always raises D-dimer in DIC.
D-dimer rises from widespread microvascular fibrinolysis in DIC, without any DVT.
D-dimer is produced when fibrin clots are broken down, which is happening widely.

steps.x: **A. Markedly raised.** DIC: high D-dimer, low fibrinogen, low platelets, prolonged PT and APTT.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman with biliary sepsis has new bruising on her arms and is oozing from a blood test site. Her temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 108 bpm and BP 100/62 mmHg. A full blood count and blood film are sent first-line.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on her full blood count?
questions.e: DIC consumes platelets in microthrombi, so the FBC shows a low platelet count, and the film may show schistocytes. A high platelet count would argue against DIC.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on her full blood count? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: oozing from a blood test site
steps.x: Sepsis with **bruising and oozing**: DIC consuming platelets.

elim: Platelets are consumed in DIC, so they fall.
Suggests allergy, parasites or drug reaction.
Suggests viral infection or chronic lymphocytic leukaemia.
Haemoglobin tends to fall with bleeding and haemolysis.

steps.x: **E. Thrombocytopenia.** First-line: FBC and blood film, looking for low platelets and schistocytes.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man with septic DIC from pneumonia is improving on intravenous antibiotics and fluids. He is no longer bleeding. The intensive care team wants to know whether his DIC is resolving.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to monitor his DIC?
o: Repeat coagulation screen and platelet count
questions.e: Management of DIC includes monitoring the coagulation profile, so serial coagulation screens and platelet counts show whether it is resolving. Blood cultures and imaging monitor the infection instead.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate investigation to monitor his DIC? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
The question is about **monitoring the coagulopathy**.

elim: Not needed to monitor DIC.
Monitors the pneumonia, not the coagulopathy.
Monitors the infection, not the coagulopathy.
Used for unexplained venous thrombosis, not DIC monitoring.

steps.x: **D. Repeat coagulation screen and platelet count.** Supportive care: IV fluids and monitoring of organ function and the coagulation profile.

questions.stem: A 42 year old woman with DIC after a postpartum haemorrhage is still bleeding despite red cells, platelets and fresh frozen plasma. Her pulse rate is 124 bpm and BP 88/50 mmHg. The haematologist asks for one result to decide whether cryoprecipitate is needed.
questions.q: Which investigation result best guides the use of cryoprecipitate?
questions.e: Cryoprecipitate is used in bleeding DIC to replace fibrinogen, so the fibrinogen level guides it. The platelet count guides platelets and the APTT and PT guide FFP.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which investigation result best guides the use of cryoprecipitate? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: still bleeding despite red cells, platelets and fresh frozen plasma
steps.x: Cryoprecipitate is given to **replace fibrinogen**.

elim: Guides fresh frozen plasma rather than cryoprecipitate.
Guides red cell transfusion.
A marker of haemolysis, not a guide to blood products.
Guides platelet transfusion.

steps.x: **E. Serum fibrinogen level.** Bleeding DIC: platelets, FFP and cryoprecipitate (for fibrinogen replacement).

questions.stem: A 35 year old man is diagnosed with acute promyelocytic leukaemia complicated by DIC. He has mild gum oozing. His platelets are 45 ×10⁹/L and fibrinogen 1.6 g/L. His pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg. He has no fever and blood cultures are negative.
questions.q: Which is the most important step in treating his DIC?
questions.e: DIC is managed first by treating the underlying cause, which here is the leukaemia. Antibiotics are for septic DIC, and heparin risks bleeding.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most important step in treating his DIC? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: acute promyelocytic leukaemia complicated by DIC
no fever and blood cultures are negative
steps.x: DIC is driven by the **leukaemia**, not infection.

elim: Anticoagulation risks severe bleeding and does not remove the trigger.
Does not address the cause and may promote thrombosis in DIC.
He has no infection; antibiotics treat septic DIC.
Has no role in DIC.

steps.x: **E. Start treatment of the leukaemia.** First-line: treat the underlying cause (antibiotics for sepsis, delivery for obstetric, treat the cancer).

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman with septic DIC from a urinary source is bleeding from her central line site and gums. Her pulse rate is 116 bpm and BP 96/58 mmHg. She is on intravenous antibiotics. Investigations: platelets 82 ×10⁹/L (150–400), PT 15 s (10–13), APTT 38 s (25–35), fibrinogen 0.6 g/L (1.5–4.0).
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate blood product to give?
questions.e: Bleeding DIC is treated with blood products targeted to the deficit; with a very low fibrinogen, cryoprecipitate is given to replace it. Her platelets and clotting times are less deranged.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate blood product to give? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: bleeding from her central line site
steps.x: Bleeding with a **very low fibrinogen**, modest platelets and near-normal clotting times.

elim: Expands volume but does not replace clotting factors.
Contains fibrinogen but in lower concentration; the main deficit here is fibrinogen.
Her platelet count is not the main problem.
Used to reverse warfarin, not to replace fibrinogen.

steps.x: **B. Cryoprecipitate.** Cryoprecipitate is for fibrinogen replacement in bleeding DIC.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man with septic DIC from pneumonia has heavy gum bleeding and a widespread petechial rash. His pulse rate is 110 bpm and BP 100/62 mmHg. He is on intravenous antibiotics. Investigations: platelets 9 ×10⁹/L (150–400), PT 14 s (10–13), APTT 36 s (25–35), fibrinogen 1.8 g/L (1.5–4.0).
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate blood product to give?
questions.e: He is actively bleeding with a platelet count of 9, so platelets are needed. His fibrinogen is normal and clotting times only slightly prolonged, so cryoprecipitate and FFP are not the priority.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate blood product to give? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Active bleeding with **severe thrombocytopenia** and near-normal clotting and fibrinogen.

elim: His fibrinogen is normal.
His PT and APTT are only slightly prolonged.
Used to reverse warfarin.
His problem is bleeding from low platelets, and no haemoglobin is given to suggest anaemia.

steps.x: **C. Platelets.** Bleeding DIC: give the product that matches the deficit (platelets, FFP or cryoprecipitate).

questions.stem: A 46 year old woman has DIC after major trauma and is oozing from her wounds and cannula sites. Her pulse rate is 112 bpm and BP 102/64 mmHg. Investigations: platelets 96 ×10⁹/L (150–400), PT 26 s (10–13), APTT 68 s (25–35), fibrinogen 1.7 g/L (1.5–4.0).
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate blood product to give?
questions.e: Fresh frozen plasma replaces consumed clotting factors when PT and APTT are markedly prolonged in bleeding DIC. Her fibrinogen and platelets are not the main deficit.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate blood product to give? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: oozing from her wounds and cannula sites
steps.x: Bleeding with **markedly prolonged PT and APTT** but fibrinogen and platelets acceptable.

elim: Her fibrinogen is not low.
Her platelet count is not low enough to explain the bleeding.
Used for warfarin reversal.
Used for haemophilia A.

steps.x: **B. Fresh frozen plasma.** FFP replaces the consumed clotting factors.

questions.stem: A 76 year old woman has septic shock from pyelonephritis. Her bloods show DIC, with platelets 58 ×10⁹/L and low fibrinogen, but she is not bleeding. Her temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 84/50 mmHg and urine output 15 mL/hour. Blood cultures have been taken.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Intravenous antibiotics, intravenous fluids and monitoring
questions.e: Without bleeding, DIC is managed by treating the cause (antibiotics) with supportive IV fluids and monitoring of organ function and coagulation. Blood products are reserved for active bleeding.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Septic DIC without bleeding**: treat the sepsis and support the circulation.

elim: Not indicated in DIC without bleeding and may worsen thrombosis.
Not given prophylactically at this count when she is not bleeding.
Not first-line and risks bleeding.
She is not bleeding; blood products are for active bleeding.

steps.x: **A. Intravenous antibiotics, intravenous fluids and monitoring.** Treat the cause and give supportive care with IV fluids and monitoring of organs and clotting.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man has a crush injury to both legs after a building collapse. Within hours he develops DIC. The trauma consultant explains that damaged tissue releases a protein that binds factor VII and starts the coagulation cascade throughout the circulation.
questions.q: Which substance is the consultant describing?
questions.e: Tissue factor released from damaged tissue binds factor VII and triggers widespread coagulation, which is how trauma, sepsis, malignancy and obstetric events cause DIC. tPA activates fibrinolysis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which substance is the consultant describing? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
The initiator of the extrinsic pathway that **binds factor VII**.

elim: A natural anticoagulant that is consumed, not the initiator.
A natural anticoagulant, not an initiator.
Activates fibrinolysis, not coagulation.
Mediates platelet adhesion and carries factor VIII; it does not bind factor VII.

steps.x: **C. Tissue factor.** DIC is triggered by tissue factor release in sepsis, trauma, malignancy and obstetric catastrophe.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman has septic DIC. Her bone marrow is working normally, but over 24 hours her platelets fall from 180 to 35 ×10⁹/L and she starts to bleed from her cannula sites, even though microthrombi are forming in her small vessels.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her bleeding?
o: Consumption of platelets and clotting factors faster than replacement
questions.e: In DIC, platelets and clotting factors are consumed by microthrombi faster than they can be replaced, leaving too little for normal haemostasis elsewhere, so she clots and bleeds at once.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely mechanism of her bleeding? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Clotting **and** bleeding together: platelets and factors are **used up** in microthrombi.

elim: Describes immune thrombocytopenia.
Her marrow is working normally.
Natural anticoagulants are consumed, not overproduced, in DIC.
Requires an enlarged spleen and does not explain microthrombi.

steps.x: **C. Consumption of platelets and clotting factors faster than replacement.** Consumption outstrips production, leaving too little for normal haemostasis elsewhere.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man with septic DIC has a haemoglobin falling from 128 to 96 g/L without obvious blood loss. His LDH is raised, haptoglobin is low and the direct antiglobulin test is negative. His blood film shows fragmented red cells.
questions.q: Which type of anaemia does he have?
questions.e: In DIC, microthrombi mechanically fragment red cells passing through partly blocked vessels, causing a microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia with schistocytes. A negative DAT excludes autoimmune haemolysis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which type of anaemia does he have? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Haemolysis, **negative DAT** and **schistocytes**: red cells are being cut up in small vessels.

elim: Develops slowly, without haemolysis or fragmented cells.
The direct antiglobulin test is negative.
Causes microcytic cells from chronic blood loss, not fragments with haemolysis.
Due to B12 or folate deficiency with macrocytes.

steps.x: **E. Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia.** Microthrombi fragment red cells: schistocytes = microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman develops DIC after a placental abruption. Her D-dimer is 18 mg/L (<0.5) and her fibrinogen is 0.5 g/L (1.5–4.0). A medical student asks why one is so high while the other is so low.
questions.q: Which best explains the raised D-dimer?
questions.e: D-dimer is a breakdown product of cross-linked fibrin, so it rises as plasmin breaks down the clots formed in DIC, while fibrinogen falls from consumption.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which best explains the raised D-dimer? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Fibrinogen is **used up** making clots; those clots are then **broken down**.

elim: Fibrinogen is low, and D-dimer is not made by the liver.
Platelets do not release D-dimer.
Not the reason D-dimer rises in DIC.
D-dimer comes from fibrin breakdown, not the placenta.

steps.x: **A. Fibrinolysis of cross-linked fibrin clots.** D-dimer reflects fibrinolysis of clots; fibrinogen is low from consumption.
